questions.title: Four components
questions.text: Name the **four** main components of the von Neumann architecture.

scheme.mark_scheme: CPU, main memory (1); input/output devices, system bus (1). 2 correct = 1 mark, 4 correct = 2 marks.
scheme.model_answer:
1 CPU
2 Main memory
3 Input/output devices
4 System bus

questions.title: Stored program concept
questions.text: Explain the **stored program concept**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A program must be stored / loaded in main memory to be executed; instructions and data are held in the same memory (1)
- the CPU fetches, decodes and executes the instructions one at a time / in sequence (1)
scheme.model_answer: A program and its data must be stored in main memory before it can run; the CPU then fetches, decodes and executes the instructions one at a time.

questions.title: Running a program
questions.text:
Put the steps of running a program in order:

- **A** The CPU fetches the first instruction from RAM
- **B** The program is stored on the SSD
- **C** The control unit decodes the instruction
- **D** The operating system loads the program into RAM

scheme.mark_scheme: B, D, A, C (1 each)

questions.title: Types of peripheral
questions.text: Tick (✓) the type of each peripheral.

scheme.mark_scheme: Input; output; storage; input; output; storage (1 each)

questions.title: Driver and controller
questions.text: Describe the role of each when a new printer is connected to a computer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Driver: software that lets the OS communicate with the printer / translates OS commands into signals the printer understands (1). Controller: hardware interface between the system bus and the printer that manages data flow / timing / buffering (1)
scheme.model_answer: Device driver: software that translates the operating system's print commands into instructions this printer understands. I/O controller: hardware that connects the printer to the system bus and manages the flow and timing of the data.

questions.title: Ports
questions.text: Match each port or connection to its typical use.

questions.title: Polling or interrupts
questions.text: Explain why interrupts are more efficient than polling for communicating with peripherals.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Polling: the CPU repeatedly checks every device, wasting processor time on devices that need nothing (1)
- Interrupts: the device signals the CPU only when it needs attention, so the CPU does other work meanwhile (1)
scheme.model_answer: With polling the CPU keeps checking each device even when nothing has happened, wasting time; with interrupts a device only signals when it needs attention, so the CPU can do other work.

questions.title: Handling an interrupt
questions.text:
Put the steps of handling an interrupt in order:

- **A** The interrupt service routine is run
- **B** The CPU checks for interrupts at the end of the fetch–decode–execute cycle
- **C** The saved register values are restored and the program continues
- **D** The contents of the registers are saved

scheme.mark_scheme: B, D, A, C (1 each)

questions.title: Causes of interrupts
questions.text: Select the **three** events that cause an interrupt.

options.content: A key is pressed on the keyboard
The printer runs out of paper
The CPU adds two numbers in the ALU
A program tries to divide by zero
The PC is incremented during fetch

scheme.mark_scheme: A, B, D
scheme.explanation: C and E are normal steps of executing instructions.

questions.title: Printing with a buffer
questions.text: Describe how a buffer and interrupts are used when a long document is printed, so that the user can carry on working.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): CPU sends part of the document to the printer buffer; CPU returns to other tasks; printer prints from the buffer at its own speed; when the buffer is empty the printer sends an interrupt; CPU saves its task / refills the buffer and returns; repeats until the document is printed
scheme.model_answer: The CPU fills the printer buffer with part of the document and goes back to other tasks. The printer prints from the buffer at its own speed. When the buffer is empty it sends an interrupt; the CPU pauses its task, refills the buffer and carries on. This repeats until the whole document is printed.

questions.title: Keyboard buffer
questions.text: Which data structure is used for the keyboard buffer so that keys are processed in the order they were pressed?

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: ALU and CU
questions.text: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) and Control Unit (CU) are components of the Central Processing Unit. Describe their purpose.

scheme.mark_scheme: ALU: processes and manipulates data; carries out arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logic (AND, OR, NOT) operations (1). CU: manages the execution of instructions; directs the processor; tells memory, ALU and I/O devices how to respond (1). Accept any reasonable answer.
scheme.model_answer:
ALU: carries out arithmetic and logic operations on data.
CU: manages the execution of instructions and sends control signals to memory, the ALU and I/O devices.

questions.title: Registers
questions.text: Match each register to what it holds.

right.text: Address of the memory location to be read or written
Data or instruction transferred to or from memory

questions.title: The fetch phase
questions.text: Describe the **fetch** phase of the fetch–decode–execute cycle, naming the registers and buses used.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): address in PC copied to MAR; MAR places address on the address bus; CU sends memory read signal on the control bus; instruction returns on the data bus into the MDR; instruction copied to the CIR; PC incremented
scheme.model_answer: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR and put on the address bus. The control unit sends a memory-read signal on the control bus. The instruction comes back on the data bus into the MDR, is copied into the CIR, and the PC is incremented.

questions.title: The three buses
questions.text: Tick (✓) the bus described by each statement.

prefill: Carries the memory read and write signals
Carries the instruction from RAM to the MDR
Carries the location of the data from the MAR

scheme.mark_scheme: Control; data; address (1 each)

questions.title: Von Neumann bottleneck
questions.text: Explain what is meant by the **von Neumann bottleneck** and describe **one** way modern processors reduce its effect.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Instructions and data share the same memory / bus (1)
- only one can be transferred at a time, so the CPU waits for memory / throughput limited (1)
- reduced by cache / pipelining / multiple cores / wider buses / Harvard-style separate caches (1)
scheme.model_answer: Instructions and data use the same path between the CPU and memory, so they cannot be transferred at the same time and the CPU often waits for memory. Cache memory reduces this by keeping frequently used data close to the CPU.

questions.title: Clock speed
questions.text: A CPU with a higher clock speed is always faster than a CPU with a lower clock speed.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Cache, number of cores, architecture and memory latency also affect performance.

questions.title: Volatile memory
questions.text: Define the term *volatile memory*.

scheme.mark_scheme: Computer memory that loses its contents when the power is turned off (1)
scheme.model_answer: Memory that loses its contents when the power is turned off.

questions.title: RAM or ROM
questions.text: Tick (✓) whether each statement describes RAM or ROM.

prefill: Contents are lost when the power is switched off
Holds the programs that are currently running
Contents are normally only read, not changed
Usually has a capacity of several gigabytes

scheme.mark_scheme: RAM; ROM; RAM; ROM; RAM (1 each)

questions.title: Why ROM is needed
questions.text: Explain why a computer needs ROM as well as RAM.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- RAM is volatile / empty when the computer is switched on (1)
- ROM keeps the boot program (BIOS/UEFI) that tests the hardware and loads the OS into RAM (1)
scheme.model_answer: When the computer is switched on RAM is empty, so the boot program stored in non-volatile ROM is needed to start the computer and load the operating system into RAM.

questions.title: Washing machine
questions.text: Embedded systems for domestic appliances (e.g. a washing machine) often have both ROM and RAM. Explain why each is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme: ROM: stores the control program / washing programmes (1) which must not change and must be kept when the power is off (1). RAM: stores the user's input (1), e.g. the chosen spin speed / washing programme / temperature / time left / sensor readings, which change each wash (1)
scheme.model_answer: ROM: holds the control program for all the washing programmes, which never changes and is kept without power. RAM: stores the user's choices such as the spin speed and temperature, and the time remaining, which change for every wash.

questions.title: SRAM and DRAM
questions.text: Tick (✓) the type of RAM each statement describes.

prefill: Must be refreshed thousands of times per second
Cheaper, so used for main memory

scheme.mark_scheme: SRAM; DRAM; DRAM (1 each)

questions.title: Purpose of virtual memory
questions.text: The operating system uses the concept of virtual memory to store some of the data. Explain the purpose of virtual memory.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): frees up space in RAM; increases the memory available beyond the physical RAM; allows more programs / multiple tasks to run at once; allows larger programs to run
scheme.model_answer: It frees up space in RAM by moving unused data to the disk, so more memory is available than the physical RAM and more programs can run at once.

questions.title: Not enough memory
questions.text: A computer shows the message **"Not enough memory to complete this operation"**. Suggest **one** way to prevent this error.

scheme.mark_scheme: Increase RAM / increase virtual memory (page file) / reduce application cache sizes / close some programs (1)
scheme.model_answer: Install more RAM.

questions.title: Disk thrashing
questions.text: Explain what disk thrashing is, why it happens and how it can be stopped.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The computer spends more time moving pages between RAM and disk than running programs (1)
- happens when RAM is too small for the programs open, so virtual memory is used constantly (1)
- fix: add more RAM / close programs (1)
scheme.model_answer: Disk thrashing is when the computer keeps swapping pages between RAM and the disk and has little time left to run programs. It happens because RAM is too small for the open programs. Adding RAM or closing programs stops it.

questions.title: Paging
questions.text:
Complete the sentences using **RAM**, **page file** or **pages**.

Programs and data are divided into [[1]]. When RAM is full, the OS moves unused ones to the [[2]] on the disk. When they are needed again they are moved back into [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) pages (2) page file (3) RAM

questions.title: Why cache is faster
questions.text: Explain why access to data in cache memory is faster than access to data in RAM.

scheme.mark_scheme: Cache is located closer to / in the CPU (1) which reduces the time to access data (1); OR cache is much smaller so data is found faster (1)(1); OR cache uses SRAM (1) with lower latency / no refresh (1)
scheme.model_answer: Cache is built into (or next to) the CPU, so the data travels a much shorter distance and is reached in less time.

questions.title: Cache hit and miss
questions.text: Explain each term.

scheme.mark_scheme: Hit: the data the CPU needs is found in the cache and used immediately (1). Miss: the data is not in the cache and must be fetched from RAM (then copied into the cache) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Cache hit: the required data is already in the cache. Cache miss: it is not, so it must be fetched from the slower RAM.

questions.title: Cache levels
questions.text: Which statement about L1 cache is correct?

options.content: It is the largest and slowest level of cache
It is the smallest and fastest level, inside each core
It is part of the hard disk
It is shared by all computers on a network

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Larger cache
questions.text: Explain how increasing the size of the cache affects the performance of the CPU.

scheme.mark_scheme: More data / instructions can be held in the cache → more cache hits (1); fewer slow accesses to RAM, so the CPU waits less and performance improves (1)
scheme.model_answer: More instructions and data fit in the cache, so there are more cache hits and fewer slow trips to RAM, making the CPU faster.

questions.title: Memory hierarchy
questions.text: Put the memory types in order from **fastest (1)** to **slowest (4)**: **RAM, registers, HDD, cache**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Registers; cache; RAM; HDD (1 each)

questions.title: A gaming laptop
questions.text: A gaming laptop has a 3.5 GHz CPU with 12 MB of L3 cache, 8 GB of RAM and a 1 TB SSD. Games often freeze when several programs are open.

parts.title: Cause
parts.text: Explain why the games freeze when several programs are open.

scheme.mark_scheme: RAM is full so virtual memory on the SSD is used (1); moving pages between RAM and disk is slow / thrashing (1)
scheme.model_answer: The 8 GB of RAM is full, so the OS moves pages to virtual memory on the SSD; swapping them back and forth is much slower than RAM, so the game freezes.

parts.title: Upgrade
parts.text: Recommend **one** hardware upgrade and explain how it solves the problem.

scheme.mark_scheme: More RAM (1); more programs and data fit in RAM so less virtual memory / swapping is needed (1)
scheme.model_answer: Upgrade to 16 GB of RAM, so all the programs fit in main memory and the computer no longer needs to swap to the SSD.

parts.title: Cache
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the 12 MB L3 cache.

scheme.mark_scheme: Stores copies of frequently used data / instructions (1) so the CPU does not have to wait for slower RAM (1)
scheme.model_answer: It keeps copies of frequently used data and instructions so the CPU can get them faster than from RAM.

questions.title: Von Neumann architecture
questions.text: Modern computer systems use the architecture proposed by John von Neumann.

parts.title: Components
parts.text: Name the **four** main components of the von Neumann architecture.

scheme.mark_scheme: CPU, main memory (1); input/output devices, system bus (1)
scheme.model_answer:
1 CPU
2 Main memory
3 Input/output devices
4 System bus

parts.title: Stored program
parts.text: Explain the stored program concept.

scheme.mark_scheme: Program and data must be stored in main memory to be executed (1); instructions fetched, decoded and executed one at a time (1)
scheme.model_answer: A program and its data must be held in main memory, where the CPU fetches, decodes and executes the instructions one at a time.

parts.title: ALU and CU
parts.text: Describe the purpose of the ALU and the CU.

scheme.mark_scheme: ALU: arithmetic and logic operations / processes data (1). CU: manages execution of instructions / sends control signals (1)
scheme.model_answer:
ALU: carries out arithmetic and logic operations.
CU: manages the execution of instructions and sends control signals to the other components.

parts.title: Fetch
parts.text: Describe the fetch phase of the fetch–decode–execute cycle, including the registers and buses used.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four (1 each): PC → MAR; address on the address bus; memory read signal on the control bus; instruction on the data bus to the MDR; MDR → CIR; PC incremented
scheme.model_answer: The address in the PC is copied to the MAR and sent on the address bus; a memory-read signal is sent on the control bus; the instruction returns on the data bus into the MDR and is copied to the CIR; the PC is incremented.

questions.title: Peripherals
questions.text: A teacher's computer is connected to a keyboard, a printer, a projector and an external hard disk.

parts.title: Types
parts.text: Tick (✓) the type of each peripheral.

scheme.mark_scheme: Input; output; output; storage — 2 rows correct = 1 mark, 4 rows = 2 marks

parts.title: Driver
parts.text: Explain why a device driver must be installed for the new printer.

scheme.mark_scheme: The driver is software that lets the OS communicate with this specific printer (1); it translates general OS commands into the signals / commands the printer understands (1)
scheme.model_answer: The operating system does not know the commands of every printer model; the driver translates its general print commands into the exact signals this printer understands.

parts.title: Interrupts
parts.text: The printer runs out of paper. Explain how the CPU deals with the interrupt it sends.

scheme.mark_scheme: CPU checks for interrupts at the end of the current cycle (1); if priority is higher, saves registers / current state (1); runs the interrupt service routine (e.g. displays 'out of paper'), then restores registers and continues (1)
scheme.model_answer: At the end of the current fetch–decode–execute cycle the CPU sees the interrupt, saves its registers, runs the interrupt service routine that shows an 'out of paper' message, then restores the registers and continues the previous task.

parts.title: Buffer
parts.text: Explain how a printer buffer allows the teacher to keep working while a long document is printed.

scheme.mark_scheme: CPU sends data to the buffer and returns to other tasks (1); printer prints from the buffer at its own speed (1); printer sends an interrupt when the buffer is empty so the CPU refills it (1)
scheme.model_answer: The CPU puts part of the document into the buffer and returns to the teacher's work; the printer prints from the buffer at its own slow speed and sends an interrupt when it is empty, so the CPU refills it.

questions.title: Main memory
questions.text: Main memory is the primary storage where the operating system, application programs and data currently being processed are stored for quick access by the CPU.

parts.title: Volatile
parts.text: Define the term *volatile memory*.

scheme.mark_scheme: Memory that loses its contents when the power is turned off (1)
scheme.model_answer: Memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off.

parts.title: RAM vs ROM
parts.text: Explain **three** differences between RAM and ROM.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three, both sides (1 each): volatile vs non-volatile; read/write vs read only; running programs and data vs boot program / firmware; large vs small capacity; contents change constantly vs set by manufacturer
scheme.model_answer: 1 RAM is volatile, whereas ROM keeps its contents without power. 2 RAM can be read and written, whereas ROM is normally only read. 3 RAM holds the running programs and data, whereas ROM holds the boot program.

parts.title: Embedded system
parts.text: Explain why the embedded system in a microwave oven needs RAM.

scheme.mark_scheme: To store the user's input (1), e.g. the cooking time and power level chosen, which change each time (1)
scheme.model_answer: To store the user's input, such as the cooking time and heat setting, which is different every time the oven is used.

parts.title: Virtual memory
parts.text: Explain the purpose of virtual memory.

scheme.mark_scheme: Frees up space in RAM (1); increases the memory available beyond physical RAM / allows more programs to run at once (1)
scheme.model_answer: It frees up space in RAM by moving unused pages to the disk, so more memory is available and more programs can run at the same time.

parts.title: Problem
parts.text: Explain **one** problem that may arise when using virtual memory.

scheme.mark_scheme: System slowdown (1) because much time is spent moving data between RAM and disk / disk is slower than RAM (1); OR increased wear on the HDD/SSD (1) because of frequent reads and writes (1)
scheme.model_answer: The computer slows down, because a lot of time is spent moving data between RAM and the disk, which is much slower than RAM.

questions.title: Cache memory
questions.text: Processor A has 4 MB of cache and processor B has 16 MB of cache. Both run at 3.2 GHz.

parts.title: Purpose
parts.text: Describe the purpose of cache memory.

scheme.mark_scheme: Stores copies of frequently used data / instructions (1) so the CPU does not have to wait for slower RAM / faster access (1)
scheme.model_answer: Cache holds copies of frequently used instructions and data close to the CPU, so they can be accessed faster than from RAM.

parts.title: Why faster
parts.text: Explain why access to data in cache memory is faster than access to data in RAM.

scheme.mark_scheme: Cache closer to / in the CPU (1), reducing access time (1); OR smaller, so faster to search (1)(1); OR uses SRAM with lower latency (1)(1)
scheme.model_answer: Cache is located inside the CPU, so the data travels a shorter distance and is reached in less time than RAM.

parts.title: Hit and miss
parts.text: Describe what happens when the CPU needs data, for a cache hit and for a cache miss.

scheme.mark_scheme: CPU checks the cache first; hit — data found and used immediately (1); miss — data fetched from RAM and a copy placed in the cache (1)
scheme.model_answer: The CPU looks in the cache first. On a hit the data is used straight away; on a miss it is fetched from RAM and a copy is stored in the cache for next time.

parts.title: Compare
parts.text: Explain which processor is likely to perform better and why.

scheme.mark_scheme: Processor B (1); larger cache holds more data → more hits, fewer slow RAM accesses (1)
scheme.model_answer: Processor B: its larger cache holds more data and instructions, so there are more cache hits and fewer slow accesses to RAM.

parts.title: Hierarchy
parts.text: Order the memories from fastest (1) to slowest (4): **SSD, cache, RAM, registers**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Registers, cache, RAM, SSD — 2 correct = 1 mark, all correct = 2 marks

summary: The von Neumann architecture and the stored program concept; the parts of a computer system and how they are connected; types of peripherals, ports, device drivers and I/O controllers; how the CPU communicates with peripherals using polling, interrupts, buffers, spooling and DMA; the functions of the CPU (control unit, ALU, registers, clock), the system bus and RAM; RAM and ROM (DRAM, SRAM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash, the boot process, embedded systems); virtual memory and paging; cache memory (levels, hits and misses, locality); the memory hierarchy and secondary storage.

blocks.content: A **stored-program** computer model: program **instructions and data are held together in main memory**. The CPU **fetches** instructions from memory, **decodes** and **executes** them one at a time, and communicates with memory and input/output devices through **buses**. It was described by **John von Neumann** in 1945 and is used by almost all general-purpose computers.

blocks.title: Core rule
blocks.content: A program must be **loaded into main memory** before the CPU can execute its instructions.

blocks.alt: Block diagram: Memory at the top connected by two-way arrows to the Control Unit and the Arithmetic Logic Unit; the Control Unit and ALU exchange signals; the ALU contains the Accumulator, which receives data from Input and sends results to Output.
blocks.caption: Von Neumann architecture: memory, control unit, ALU with accumulator, input and output

blocks.content: A computer system **takes in data (input)**, **processes** it, **stores** it and **produces results (output)**. In the **von Neumann architecture**, used by almost all computers, these jobs are done by four groups of components connected by the **system bus**.

blocks.caption: The main components of a computer system

blocks.title: Components and their jobs
rows: **Fetches, decodes and executes** program instructions; processes data; controls the other components
Holds the **programs and data the CPU is using now** (RAM) and the start-up instructions (ROM)
Carries **addresses**, **data** and **control signals** between the CPU, memory and I/O controllers
Electronic interfaces that connect **peripherals** to the system bus
Devices **outside** the CPU and main memory: input, output and secondary storage

blocks.content: If you are asked to **name the four main components** of the von Neumann architecture, write: **CPU, main memory, input/output devices, system bus**.

blocks.alt: The CPU (control unit, ALU and registers), main memory and the I/O devices disk and printer are all connected to one shared bus.
blocks.caption: CPU, main memory and I/O devices sharing one bus

blocks.title: Input, process, output
blocks.content: The simplest view of what a computer does: the input value **10** enters the system, the processor executes an instruction to **multiply it by 3**, and the result **30** becomes the output. One input may lead to **several processes and outputs** (the result could also be stored or printed).

blocks.alt: Three boxes connected by arrows: Input 10, Process multiply by 3, Output 30.
blocks.caption: Input 10 → Process: multiply by 3 → Output 30

blocks.content: A program must be **stored in main memory** in order to be executed. Its **instructions and the data** it uses are kept in the **same memory**, and the CPU **fetches, decodes and executes** the instructions **one at a time**, following the instruction sequence (unless a jump changes the order).

blocks.title: From storage to results
items: **Secondary storage** — the program is kept permanently on an SSD, hard disk, USB drive or optical disc.
**Main memory** — the operating system **copies** the program's instructions and the data it needs into **RAM**.
**Processor** — the CPU fetches, decodes and executes the instructions from RAM.
**Output / storage** — the results are displayed, printed or saved back to secondary storage.

blocks.alt: Hard disk, USB drive and DVD/Blu-ray in a secondary storage group, with an arrow to Main Memory, which exchanges data in both directions with the Processor.
blocks.caption: A program is loaded from secondary storage into main memory, then executed by the processor

blocks.title: Why the program must be copied into RAM
blocks.content: **RAM is volatile** — it loses its contents when the power is removed — so programs and files are kept long term on **secondary storage**. But secondary storage is far too **slow** for the CPU to fetch instructions from directly, so **loading** a program means copying the code and data it needs from secondary storage into **RAM**.

blocks.title: Running a program from storage
blocks.content:
- A program is stored on an SSD, hard disk, USB drive or optical disc.
- The **operating system** loads the required instructions and data into **RAM**.
- The CPU **fetches** the first instruction from RAM.
- The **control unit** decodes the instruction.
- The CPU **executes** it.
- The cycle **repeats** until the program finishes or branches elsewhere.
A hardware device **outside the CPU and main memory** that is connected to the computer to **input**, **output** or **store** data. Peripherals are much **slower** than the CPU.

blocks.title: Types of peripheral
rows: Enter data and commands into the computer
Keyboard, mouse, touch screen, microphone, scanner, webcam, barcode reader, sensors (temperature, light, motion)
Present results to the user or control other devices
Monitor, printer, speakers, headphones, projector, actuators (motors, valves), LEDs
Hard disk drive (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), USB flash drive, memory card, optical disc
Connect the computer to other devices and networks
Network interface card, Wi-Fi adapter, modem, Bluetooth adapter
Touch screen, headset with microphone, multifunction printer/scanner

blocks.title: Ports and connections
rows: Keyboard, mouse, flash drive, printer, phone
Universal; also supplies **power**; USB-C carries data, video and charging

blocks.content: A **physical connection point** (or logical interface) where a peripheral's cable or wireless interface connects to the computer — for example a USB, HDMI or Ethernet port. The **I/O controller** behind the port manages the flow of information between the device and the processor.

items.title: Device drivers
items.content:
- A **device driver** is **software** that lets the **operating system** communicate with one particular hardware device.
- It **translates** general OS commands ("print this page") into the exact signals the device understands, and passes the device's messages (errors, status) back.
- New hardware usually needs its driver installed; **plug and play** devices are recognised and set up automatically.

items.title: I/O controllers
items.content:
- An **I/O controller** (interface) is **hardware** — a circuit board or chip — between the system bus and a device.
- It converts data to the **form and speed** the device needs, has its own small **buffer** and signals the CPU when the device needs attention.
- Examples: USB controller, graphics card (video controller), disk controller, network card.

blocks.title: Typical data flow
rows: The **keyboard controller** detects a key press, **encodes** it as a key code and makes it available; it raises an **interrupt**; the CPU reads the data through the I/O interface and the **bus system**
The CPU sends the data and **control information** to the **printer controller**; the controller manages the **timing** of the printer and sends it suitable signals; the printed page is the output

blocks.title: Why controllers are needed
blocks.content: Peripherals work at **different speeds** and use **different protocols** from the CPU. Controllers **bridge** this difference: they convert the data, **buffer** it and use **interrupts** so the CPU does not have to check the device continuously.

theory.title: How the CPU communicates with peripherals

blocks.content: The CPU is **millions of times faster** than a printer or a person typing. If it waited for each device it would waste almost all its time. Several techniques let the CPU and the peripherals work **at their own speeds**.

blocks.title: Polling vs interrupts
rows: The CPU **checks each device in turn**, again and again, to see if it needs attention
The **device sends a signal** to the CPU only when it needs attention
**Wasted** checking devices that do not need anything
Used for other work until a device interrupts
Delayed until the device's turn comes

blocks.content: A **signal** sent to the CPU from **hardware** (key pressed, mouse moved, printer out of paper, data arrived from the network), from **software** (an error such as division by zero, a request to the OS) or from a **timer**, telling the CPU that something **needs attention**.

blocks.title: How the CPU handles an interrupt
items: The device sends an interrupt signal along the **control bus**; it is stored in the **interrupt register**.
At the **end of each fetch–decode–execute cycle** the CPU checks for interrupts.
If the interrupt has a **higher priority** than the current task, the CPU **saves the contents of its registers** (PC, ACC …) on the **stack**.
The CPU runs the **interrupt service routine (ISR)** — the code that deals with this interrupt (e.g. reads the key code).
The saved register values are **restored** and the CPU **continues** the interrupted program exactly where it stopped.
A lower-priority interrupt waits until the current task or a more urgent interrupt is finished.

blocks.content: An area of **memory** that holds data **temporarily** while it is being moved between two devices that work at **different speeds** — for example between the CPU / RAM and a printer, or between the network and a video player.

blocks.title: Printing a document with a buffer and interrupts
items: The CPU sends the first part of the document to the **printer buffer** in RAM and **returns to other tasks**.
The printer takes data from the buffer and prints it at its own (slow) speed.
When the buffer is **empty**, the printer sends an **interrupt** asking for more data.
The CPU suspends its current task, **refills the buffer**, and returns to the task.
This repeats until the document is printed; the user can keep working the whole time.

items.title: Keyboard buffer
items.content:
- Each key pressed causes an **interrupt**; the key code is placed in the **keyboard buffer** (a **queue**).
- The program reads the keys **in the order typed**, even if the user types faster than it processes them.

items.title: Video streaming buffer
items.content: - Data from the Internet is stored in a buffer a few seconds ahead of what is being played, so short network delays do not stop the video.

items.title: Spooling
items.content: - Print jobs from several users are stored on **disk** in a **print queue (spool)** and sent to the printer one by one, so users do not have to wait for the printer.

items.title: Direct Memory Access (DMA)
items.content: - A **DMA controller** moves large blocks of data between a device (disk, network card) and **RAM** **without the CPU**, and interrupts the CPU only when the whole block has been transferred.

blocks.content: The part of the computer that **fetches, decodes and executes** the instructions of programs and **processes data**. It contains the **control unit**, the **arithmetic logic unit**, **registers**, **cache** and a **clock**.

blocks.title: Parts of the CPU
rows: **Manages the execution of instructions**: controls the fetch–decode–execute cycle, **decodes** instructions and sends **control signals** that tell memory, the ALU and the I/O devices what to do
**Processes data**: **arithmetic** operations (+, −, ×, ÷) and **logic** operations (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons such as >, =), shifts
Very small, extremely fast storage **inside the CPU** for the data and addresses being used **now**
Sends regular pulses that **synchronise** all operations; its speed (GHz) is the number of cycles per second
Fast memory holding copies of frequently used data and instructions

blocks.title: Clock speed is not everything
blocks.content: Clock speed is measured in **hertz** — modern CPUs run at several **gigahertz** (billions of cycles per second). A higher clock speed **alone does not guarantee** a faster CPU: performance also depends on the **architecture**, **cache** size, number of **cores**, how much work each instruction does, **memory latency** and the **workload**.

blocks.alt: Photograph of processor chips: the top and the underside of a CPU package.
blocks.caption: A physical processor package

blocks.content: Inside a modern processor are **billions of transistor switches** that implement the logic of the control unit, the ALU and the registers.

blocks.title: Main registers
rows: The **address** of the memory location to be read or written
The **data or instruction** read from, or to be written to, memory

blocks.content: Some syllabuses call the MDR the **MBR (Memory Buffer Register)**. The function is the same: it holds the data or instruction being transferred to or from memory.

blocks.title: The CPU's main cycle (fetch–decode–execute) — simple version
items: **Fetch** — retrieve the **next instruction** from main memory and bring it into the CPU.
**Decode** — the **control unit** interprets the instruction and determines what operation is required.
**Execute** — the CPU carries out the instruction: a **calculation**, a **memory access**, a **logical decision** or an **I/O operation**.
The CPU checks for **interrupts**, then repeats — billions of times per second.

blocks.alt: Cycle diagram: in the fetch cycle the control unit 1 fetches the instruction and 2 decodes it; in the execution cycle the ALU 3 gets data and 4 executes the instruction; registers sit between them and main memory is below; arrows show the cycle repeating.
blocks.caption: The fetch cycle (control unit) and the execution cycle (ALU), with registers and main memory

blocks.title: Detailed fetch phase
items: The **PC** contains the address of the next instruction.
The address is copied from the **PC** to the **MAR**.
The MAR places the address on the **address bus**.
The **control unit** sends a **memory read** signal through the **control bus**.
**RAM** locates the instruction stored at that address.
The instruction travels back to the CPU through the **data bus** and enters the **MDR**.
The instruction is copied to the **CIR** for decoding.
The **PC** advances to the address of the next instruction.

items.title: Decode phase
items.content:
- The **control unit** interprets the instruction in the **CIR**.
- It identifies the **operation (opcode)** and any required **operands**, and the **addressing mode**.
- It prepares the **control signals** needed for execution.

items.title: Execute phase
items.content: - The required action takes place: the **ALU** does arithmetic or a logic operation, data is **read into the accumulator**, a value is **written from the accumulator back to RAM**, or a **jump** changes the PC.

blocks.content: **PC → MAR → address bus → RAM → data bus → MDR → CIR → decode → execute**

blocks.title: The three buses of the system bus
rows: The **address** of the memory location or I/O port to use
**Control signals**: memory read, memory write, clock, interrupt request

blocks.title: Bus width
blocks.content: The **wider** the data bus, the more bits are moved at once (64-bit → 8 bytes per transfer). The **wider** the address bus, the more memory locations can be addressed (n lines → 2ⁿ locations).

The computer's **main working memory**. It holds the **operating system**, the **programs that are running** and the **data they are using**. "Random access" means any location can be read or written directly, in the same time, by its address.

items.title: Functions of RAM
items.content:
- Stores the **instructions** of running programs so the CPU can **fetch** them.
- Stores the **data** being processed (an open document, a game level).
- Holds **buffers** for devices and parts of the OS.
- Is **much faster** than secondary storage, so programs run quickly.

items.title: How the amount of RAM affects performance
items.content:
- **More RAM** → more programs and data fit in memory at once → **less virtual memory** is used → the computer is **faster**.
- **Too little RAM** → the OS swaps data to disk → the computer slows down, or shows "**Not enough memory**".

theory.title: Advantages and limitations of the von Neumann architecture

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- Instructions and data share **one memory system**, which **simplifies the design** and makes it cheaper.
- The control unit retrieves data and instructions through **one common mechanism** (the same buses).
- Memory is **general-purpose**: its capacity is not permanently split between program and data, so it is used **flexibly**.
- A new program can be run just by **loading it into memory** — no rewiring; suitable for **general-purpose computing**.

items.title: Limitations
items.content:
- **Von Neumann bottleneck** — instructions and data share the **same path** between the CPU and memory, so only one can be transferred at a time; this **limits throughput** and the CPU often waits for memory.
- The classical model processes **one instruction at a time, in sequence**.
- Because program instructions share memory with data, **faulty or malicious writes** to the memory holding a program can change it if there is no **memory protection**.

blocks.title: Reducing the bottleneck
blocks.content: The von Neumann bottleneck is the **throughput limitation** caused by instructions and data **sharing the memory pathway**. Modern processors reduce its practical impact with **cache memory**, **pipelining**, **branch prediction**, **multiple cores** and wider, faster buses. The **Harvard architecture** uses **separate** memories and buses for instructions and data, so both can be fetched at the same time.
Memory that **loses its contents when the power is turned off** (RAM). **Non-volatile** memory keeps its contents without power (ROM, flash, disks).

blocks.title: RAM vs ROM
rows: **Volatile** — contents lost when power is off
**Read only** (or only rarely updated, e.g. firmware update in flash)
**Boot program (BIOS / UEFI)**, firmware, fixed programs of embedded devices

blocks.title: Types of RAM
rows: Capacitors that must be **refreshed** thousands of times per second

blocks.title: Types of ROM
rows: Contents written during manufacture, cannot be changed
Programmable once by the user, then fixed
Erased and rewritten **electrically** — used for BIOS/UEFI so the firmware can be updated

blocks.title: The boot process — why ROM is needed
items: When the computer is switched on, **RAM is empty** (volatile).
The CPU starts running the **bootstrap / BIOS (UEFI)** program stored in **ROM**.
It **tests the hardware** (POST — power-on self-test) and finds the boot device.
It **loads the operating system** from secondary storage into **RAM**.
Control passes to the OS, which keeps running from RAM.

blocks.title: Embedded systems need both ROM and RAM
blocks.content:
A **washing machine** has a microcontroller with:
- **ROM** — the **control program** (all the washing programmes and how to run the motor, pump and heater); it never changes and must survive power cuts.
- **RAM** — the **user's input** and current state: chosen programme, temperature, **spin speed**, time remaining, readings from the sensors; it changes during every wash.

A microwave oven similarly keeps its program in ROM and the **time and power setting** in RAM.

A part of **secondary storage (HDD / SSD)** that the operating system uses **as if it were extra RAM** when the physical RAM is full. The file on the disk is called the **page file** or **swap file**.

items.title: Purpose of virtual memory
items.content:
- **Frees up space in RAM** for the program currently being used.
- **Increases the amount of memory available** beyond the physical RAM.
- Allows **more programs** to be open at once (**multitasking**) and **larger programs** to run than RAM alone would allow.
- Prevents programs from crashing when RAM runs out.

blocks.title: How virtual memory works (paging)
items: Programs and data are divided into fixed-size blocks called **pages**.
When RAM is full, the OS moves pages that are **not being used now** from RAM to the **page file** on the disk (**paging out / swapping out**).
When the CPU needs one of those pages, the OS moves it **back into RAM** (**paging in**), first moving another unused page out.
The program does not know where its pages are — the OS keeps a **page table**.

items.title: Problems of virtual memory
items.content:
- **Slower** — reading and writing the disk is much slower than RAM, so data processing slows down.
- **Disk thrashing** — when RAM is far too small, the computer spends more time **moving pages between RAM and disk** than running programs; it becomes very slow and the disk is constantly busy.
- More **wear** on the HDD / SSD because of frequent reads and writes.

items.title: Preventing "Not enough memory" errors and thrashing
items.content:
- **Install more RAM** (the best solution).
- **Close** programs that are not needed.
- **Increase** the size of the page file (virtual memory).
- Reduce the cache sizes of applications.

blocks.content: Very **fast, small memory** inside or next to the CPU that stores **copies of frequently used instructions and data**, so that the CPU does not have to wait for the slower RAM.

blocks.title: How the cache works
items: When the CPU needs data or an instruction, it checks the **cache first**.
**Cache hit** — the data is in the cache and is used immediately (fast).
**Cache miss** — the data is fetched from **RAM**, and a copy (with nearby data) is placed in the cache for next time.
When the cache is full, the **least recently used** data is replaced.

items.title: Why cache is faster than RAM
items.content:
- It is **physically closer** to (or inside) the CPU, so signals travel a shorter distance.
- It is made of **SRAM**, which has **lower latency** and needs no refresh.
- It is **much smaller**, so the right data is found faster.
- It runs at (or close to) the **speed of the CPU**.

items.title: Why it works — locality of reference
items.content:
- **Temporal locality** — data used recently is likely to be used again soon (a loop counter).
- **Spatial locality** — data near recently used data is likely to be needed next (the next elements of an array, the next instructions).

blocks.title: Cache levels
rows: Inside each CPU core (separate for instructions and data)
Inside each core or shared by two
Shared by all cores on the chip

blocks.title: Effect of cache size
blocks.content: A **larger** cache gives **more cache hits** and fewer slow RAM accesses, so the CPU is faster. But cache is **expensive** and takes space on the chip, and beyond a certain size the benefit becomes small.

theory.title: The memory hierarchy and secondary storage

blocks.title: Memory hierarchy (fast and small → slow and large)

blocks.content: Going **down** the hierarchy, memory becomes **slower**, **larger** and **cheaper per GB**. Going **up**, it becomes **faster**, **smaller** and **more expensive**. Each level holds copies of the data most likely to be needed by the level above.

blocks.title: Secondary storage devices
rows: Magnetised spinning platters, moving read/write head
Electrical charge in flash memory chips, **no moving parts**

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name the four main components of the von Neumann architecture. [2]**
CPU, main memory (1); input/output devices, system bus (1).

**Q: Explain what is meant by the von Neumann bottleneck. [2]**
Instructions and data share the **same memory and bus** (1), so they cannot be transferred at the same time and the CPU often **waits for memory**, limiting performance (1).

**Q: Describe the fetch stage of the cycle. [3]**
The address in the **PC** is copied to the **MAR** and sent on the **address bus** (1); a **memory read** signal is sent and the instruction returns on the **data bus** to the **MDR** (1); it is copied to the **CIR** and the **PC is incremented** (1).

**Q: Describe the purpose of the ALU and the CU. [2]**
**ALU** — processes data: carries out **arithmetic** (+, −, ×, ÷) and **logic** (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons) operations (1). **CU** — **manages the execution of instructions**: directs the processor and tells memory, the ALU and I/O devices how to respond (1).

**Q: Define the term volatile memory. [1]**
Memory that **loses its contents when the power is turned off** (1).

**Q: Explain why embedded systems such as washing machines need RAM. [2]**
To store the **user's input** (1), for example the **spin speed and washing programme** chosen, which change for each wash (1).

**Q: Explain the purpose of virtual memory. [2]**
It **frees up space in RAM** (1) and **increases the memory available** beyond the physical RAM, so more programs / tasks can run at once (1).

**Q: Explain one problem that may arise when using virtual memory. [2]**
The system **slows down** (1) because it spends much time **moving data between RAM and the disk**, which is much slower than RAM (1).

**Q: Explain why access to data in cache memory is faster than in RAM. [2]**
Cache is located **in / closer to the CPU** (1), which **reduces the time** it takes to access the data (1). (Or: cache uses **SRAM**, which has lower latency.)

**Q: Explain how an interrupt is handled. [3]**
The CPU checks for interrupts at the **end of each cycle** (1); it **saves its registers** and runs the **interrupt service routine** (1); then **restores** the registers and continues the previous task (1).

blocks.title: Key terms — one-sentence definitions
rows: A stored-program architecture where instructions and data share main memory and are processed by a CPU
The processor that executes instructions, processes data and coordinates system operations
The CPU component that manages instruction execution and sends control signals
The CPU component that performs arithmetic and logical operations
Small, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU
A timing mechanism that synchronises CPU activity
Memory holding the active program instructions and data for CPU access
The communication system linking the CPU, memory and I/O devices
The principle that a program must be stored in main memory to be executed
Get the next instruction from memory / interpret it / carry it out
Hardware that manages the flow of information between the CPU and a peripheral
A physical or logical interface used to connect a peripheral or network interface
A signal telling the CPU that a device or program needs attention
Temporary memory between devices working at different speeds

blocks.content:
- Saying ROM "is used for storing files" — files are stored on **secondary storage**; ROM holds the **boot program / firmware**.
- Saying virtual memory **makes the computer faster** — it allows more programs to run, but it is **slower** than RAM.
- Confusing **cache** (fast memory near the CPU) with **virtual memory** (disk used as RAM).
- Saying the PC holds the **current** instruction — it holds the **address of the next** one.
- Explaining the von Neumann bottleneck as "the CPU is slow" — it is the **shared path** between CPU and memory.
- Saying a device driver is hardware — it is **software**; the I/O controller is hardware.
- Writing "RAM stores data permanently" — RAM is **volatile**.
